title: How much does it really cost to study in Europe (tuition and living), country by country
summary: A method for comparing tuition, mandatory fees, living costs and one-off costs across countries, with the official figures verified so far for France and the Netherlands.

sources.title: Campus France: tuition fees in France
Study in the Netherlands: tuition fees

review_note: Verified on fetched official pages: Campus France gives €2,902 per year for non-EU bachelor's students at public institutions for 2026-2027. StudyinNL gives an average tuition range of €9,000 to €20,000 per year for non-EU/EEA bachelor's students, with no stated year. Germany: the Federal Foreign Office page gives no blocked account amount, so none is stated. Not verified and left blank in the article: living costs for every city, Italy, Spain, Poland and Finland tuition, and German public-university fee rules by state. The reader is told to fill those from official pages.
body:
## In short

- The cost of studying in Europe is tuition plus living costs. For many students, living costs are the bigger share.
- Tuition for non-EU students ranges from very low at some public universities to high at others. Read the official fee page for each country and each university.
- Official figures are set by each government or university and change each year. Use the numbers below as examples of where to look, and confirm the current year before you budget.
- Build your own budget with the same categories for every country, so you can compare like with like.

## How to compare countries fairly

Use one method for every country:

1. Tuition for the first year, from the official university or government page.
2. Mandatory fees, such as a semester contribution or student union fee.
3. Living costs, based on the city you will live in, not the national average.
4. Health insurance, which most European countries require for students from outside the EU.
5. Visa and residence costs, such as application fees and the cost of the financial proof.
6. A buffer for the first two months, when you pay deposits and buy equipment.

Keep the figures in one spreadsheet with the source and the year beside each. If you cannot find a source, leave the cell blank rather than estimating.

## France

The official Campus France site gives the 2026-2027 tuition for non-EU students at public institutions for a bachelor's programme as €2,902 per year. That is a verified figure for the year stated. Check whether your programme or university charges a different fee, and whether it is a private institution, which can cost more.

Living costs in France depend heavily on the city. Paris is the most expensive. Budget for housing, transport, food and insurance, and check the student residence and visa financial requirements on official sources before you apply.

## The Netherlands

The official Study in the Netherlands site gives an average tuition fee range of €9,000 to €20,000 per year for bachelor's programmes for students with non-EU or non-EEA nationality. The range is wide because it depends on the university and the programme. Use the university's own fee table for your specific course.

The same site notes that living costs are separate and should be budgeted from a source for your city.

## Germany

Many public universities in Germany charge no tuition for bachelor's study, but some states and some programmes charge fees to non-EU students. Most students still pay a semester contribution. Living costs and the blocked account, which the German mission sets each year, are the largest part of the budget. The official German Federal Foreign Office page says the blocked account amount varies by purpose and is set out by the competent mission. Confirm the current amount with the mission before you budget.

## Italy, Spain, Poland and Finland

Public universities in these countries differ widely. Some charge modest fees for international students, and some offer English-taught bachelor's programmes at higher fees. Finland has charged fees to many non-EU students for some years, so check the rules for the year you apply. Do not use an older table from a blog. Go to each university's international fees page and record the figure with the date you read it.

## What to do with the numbers

Once you have verified tuition for each country, add living costs for your city. Use the cost of rent in a shared flat, a monthly food estimate, transport, phone, health insurance and an entertainment allowance. Multiply by the number of months in your course, and add the one-off costs: visa fees, flights, deposits and the first month's rent.

A simple way to present the result is a table with three columns: tuition, living costs, and the one-off costs. Mark each figure with its source and year. Where a figure is missing, say so.

## Scholarships change the picture

If you hold a scholarship that covers tuition or living costs, the budget changes a lot. Read the scholarship benefits carefully, as explained in the scholarships article in this series. A scholarship that covers tuition but not housing still leaves a large gap.

## Common mistakes

- Comparing tuition for one city with living costs for another.
- Using a national average instead of a city figure.
- Forgetting mandatory fees and health insurance.
- Assuming "free tuition" means free study.
- Not updating the budget when the year changes.

## Tuition is only the first line

Students often compare tuition alone, then discover that the total is much higher. Mandatory fees can include a student services contribution, an administration fee, a library or equipment charge, or a lab fee. Some programmes also require a placement, an internship or a language course, and these may carry separate costs. Read the programme's full fee schedule and ask what is included in the stated figure.

## Living costs by type of city

Within one country the living costs can vary a lot. A capital city usually costs more than a university town. Rent is often the largest single item, and shared flats are the most common choice for students. Public transport passes, groceries and eating out differ by city, so use local sources rather than a national summary.

## Planning for the first months

The first two months often cost more than later months. You may need to pay a deposit, buy textbooks, pay the first month's rent in advance and cover the cost of registration and insurance. Keep a separate buffer for these costs. Students who run out of money early often struggle with housing and food, so this buffer is worth planning carefully.

## Currency and transfers

Exchange rates change, and transfer fees differ between banks and money services. Keep your budget in the currency the university charges, and check the rate you use. If you plan to transfer money from Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan, compare the total cost of each transfer route, including fees and the rate applied. Do not send money before you have confirmed the university's account details directly with the university.

## Part-time work and its limits

Many students plan to work part-time to cover living costs. Rules on hours, eligibility and the type of work differ by country and by visa. Treat part-time earnings as a bonus rather than a core part of the budget, and check the official rules for your visa category before you accept any job offer.

## Checking the year on every figure

A fee table is only useful for the academic year it names. Write the year next to each figure in your comparison, and if the source does not name a year, treat the figure as unverified. Academic years run from autumn to summer, so a figure for 2026-2027 may not match a figure published in a previous spring. Before you send any deposit, open the official page again and confirm that the figure still matches.

## Checklist

- [ ] Choose the cities you will compare and note the year for each figure.
- [ ] Check the official university fee page for tuition and mandatory fees.
- [ ] Check the official visa and financial requirement page for each country.
- [ ] Estimate living costs for the city, not the country.
- [ ] Add health insurance and the one-off costs.
- [ ] Record the source and date for every number.
- [ ] Recheck the figures before you send any money.
